beats.intro: Lesson twenty-six. [[sub]]How to deliver a review so the message lands, and how to prepare the usual mixed one.
beats.threel: Delivering the review is as hard as judging. Grove gives three L's. [[lev]]Level, [[lis]]listen, [[out]]and leave yourself out. [[frank]]Level means be totally frank. The credibility of the whole review system depends on it. [[praise]]And plain praise can be just as hard to give as criticism.
beats.listen: Listen has a special meaning here. [[chain]]Communication moves a thought from one brain to another. Thoughts become words, words become sound, sound reaches the ear, and the brain turns it back into thoughts. [[tape]]Should you record the review to prove what you said? Emphatically no. The words are only the means. The thought arriving is the end. [[block]]The other person may be too upset to understand, busy planning a reply, or tuned out, thinking of going fishing. [[conf]]It happens most when the message carries conflict.
beats.watch: So how do you know you were heard? [[para]]Asking them to repeat your words is not enough. [[senses]]Use all your senses. Watch them. Are their responses, spoken and unspoken, the right ones? [[keep]]If you are not sure the message got through, it is your job to keep at it. [[teach]]A good teacher knows when the class is lost, and explains again, another way. [[board]]We have all had the professor who mumbled at the blackboard, avoiding our eyes, because he knew he was unclear. Don't be that professor.
beats.leave: The third L: leave yourself out. [[about]]The review is about your report, and for your report. [[own]]Keep your own insecurity, anxiety, or guilt out of it. [[court]]It is their day in court, not yours. [[stage]]You will feel strong emotions before and during a review, like an actor's stage fright. They come back no matter how many reviews you give. Control them, so they don't steer the review.
beats.types: Grove describes three types of review. [[mixed]]The mixed one, on the one hand, on the other hand. [[blast]]The blast, for a serious problem. [[ace]]And the review of an ace. The last two are next lesson. [[most]]Most reviews are mixed, and they go wrong in familiar ways: [[sup]]superficial comments, clichés, and laundry lists of unrelated points. They leave people bewildered.
beats.capacity: The key: people can only take in so much. [[seven]]You may know seven true things about their performance. [[four]]But if they can absorb four, [[waste]]at best you waste your breath on the other three. [[over]]At worst you overload them, and they leave with nothing. [[less]]The aim is not to empty your head of every truth. It is to improve their performance. Less may be more.
beats.worksheet: So how do you choose? [[scan]]First, gather everything: progress reports, results against quarterly objectives, your one-on-one notes. [[blank]]Then take a blank sheet and write down everything you can think of. Don't edit in your head. Writing it down commits you to nothing. [[away]]When you run out, put the documents away. [[rel]]Now look for links. Several items are often signs of the same thing, and some hint at why. [[msg]]Those links become your messages, each with specific examples. [[cut]]Finally ask: will they remember them all? If not, drop the less important ones. They can wait for the next review.
beats.grovesheet: Here is Grove's own worksheet for a supervisor. [[pos]]On the plus side: the planning process much better, a good report to a council, help on a cost analysis. [[neg]]On the minus side: no progress on the specification process, meetings that turn into a debating society, a weak start to training. [[cross]]Two smaller points were crossed out. [[m1]]Message one: good results on planning, helped by a financial background. [[m2]]Message two: a hard time setting clear, crisp goals, satisfied with activity instead of results. [[m3]]A third message was struck out too: let's just concentrate on number two.
beats.surprise: What about surprises? [[ideal]]If you held regular one-on-ones all year, the review should hold none. Right? [[wrongs]]Wrong. Working through the worksheet, you may find a message that startles even you. [[deliver]]If the purpose is to improve their performance, you must deliver it. [[swallow]]Preferably no surprises. But if you find one, swallow hard and bring it up.
beats.sample: Grove then shows the written review built from that worksheet, with his notes in the margin. [[outm]]The planning work is an output measure, and it was good. [[intm]]The specification work is an internal measure that was lacking: activity, not output. [[ex]]Each criticism is backed by an example, like the mushy end of a spec review. [[comp]]And compliments need examples too: the voluntary help to purchasing. [[how]]It also shows how to improve. He wants a promotion. Not yet. First he must drive complex projects to results on his own. [[rate]]The rating: meets requirements, one he should be able to raise.
beats.signoff: Look at who signs. [[two]]Two levels of management and personnel, as checks and balances. [[dual]]It was prepared jointly with the head of a council he also served, an example of dual reporting. [[sig]]And the employee signs too. His signature means he received the review. It does not mean he agrees with it.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Level: be totally frank, in praise as well. [[w2]]Listen with every sense until you know you were heard. [[w3]]Leave yourself out: it is their day in court. [[w4]]Write everything down, find the messages, cut to a few. [[w5]]Back every point with an example, even the surprises. Now the lesson practice.
